{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01HdpX2sfhYYPGZsNwsdSk5v","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# BUILD PLAN — output format\n2\t\n3\tEmit the plan in exactly these sections, in this order. Keep it concrete: name real\n4\ttechnologies and real checks, not placeholders. Length is not quality: prefer one-line table\n5\tcells, cite IDs (V2, Phase 3, E1) instead of restating content, and scale the plan to the system.\n6\tA section with nothing load-bearing is one line (\"None.\", \"N/A — <reason>\"); a section that a\n7\tdeclared exception makes moot is one line citing it.\n8\t\n9\t---\n10\t\n11\t## 1. Classification and constraints\n12\t- **What:** one line on the system.\n13\t- **Type:** software / infra / AI-agentic (or a mix); greenfield or brownfield; small build or not.\n14\t- **Dominant constraint:** correctness | availability | latency | cost | scale | compliance.\n15\t- **Worst failure:** the single failure that would hurt most.\n16\t\n17\t**Budgets** (only the rows that bind; add rows the system needs, such as a cutover freeze window):\n18\t\n19\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n20\t|---|---|---|---|\n21\t| Latency | … | REQUIREMENT / BASELINE / ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | V… or Phase … |\n22\t| Throughput | … | … | … |\n23\t| Availability / SLO | … | … | … |\n24\t| RPO / RTO | … | … | … |\n25\t| Resource use | … | … | … |\n26\t| AI inference cost | … (AI systems only) | … | … |\n27\t| Storage cost | … | … | … |\n28\t| Operational complexity | … (e.g. services to run, on-call load) | … | … |\n29\t\n30\tAn UNKNOWN target has no number: write the missing input, who supplies it, and the phase that\n31\tneeds it. An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n47\t\n48\t| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n49\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n50\t| Consistency vs availability | R2/R3 + one-clause reason | … | … | V…, a cheap check, or the cited basis | … (for a gated row: \"V… fails, or …\") |\n51\t| Monolith vs services | … | … | … | … | … |\n52\t| Sync vs async | … | … | … | … | … |\n53\t| Build vs buy | … | … | … | … | … |\n54\t| Data-privacy boundary (personal or regulated data) | … | … | … | … | … |\n55\t| <each system-specific R2/R3 decision, e.g. the tenancy model> | … | … | … | … | … |\n56\t| (Brownfield) migration strategy, coexistence and cutover, rollback, system of record | … | … | … | … | … |\n57\t| (AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | … | … | … | … | … |\n58\t| (AI) hosted API vs self-host | … | … | … | … | … |\n59\t\n60\t**R1 defaults:** <decision> → <default>; … (one line; no rows for R1 decisions).\n61\t**N/A:** <considered decisions that do not apply> — <reason> (one line).\n62\tOmit the (Brownfield) and (AI) rows when they do not apply. Inherited brownfield decisions the\n63\tplan will not change are listed once as constraints, not as rows.\n64\t\n65\t## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n66\t- The one real request and the real response.\n67\t- Every tier it crosses.\n68\t- How it is deployed, logged, monitored, and rolled back on day zero.\n69\t- Who can reach it (internal or allow-listed traffic behind a flag until its controls exist).\n70\t\n71\tIf an exception changes Phase 0, say so in one line and cite it (E…).\n72\tExit check (V0): a real request succeeds with one trace across every tier; a deploy and a\n73\trollback succeed through the pipeline; an injected failure fires an alert; the first values of\n74\tthe measurable budgets are recorded as baselines, not targets.\n75\t\n76\t## 5. Phases (Phase 1 onward; dependency order; within a phase, rework widest first, exposure smallest first)\n77\tFor each phase:\n78\t- **Phase N — <name>**\n79\t  - Unlocks: what becomes possible after it.\n80\t  - Depends on: earlier phases and V-IDs, by reference.\n81\t  - Tasks: in order.\n82\t  - Rollback: how this phase is undone, or its point of no return and the gate that guards it.\n83\t  - Exit check: its gates pass, plus any observable condition that no gate covers.\n84\t\n85\t## 6. Validation gates\n86\t\n87\t| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n88\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n89\t| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed, and rolled back through every tier in production | … | the V0 exit check in §4 | … | Phase 1 | 0 |\n90\t| V1 | … | … | … (labeled) | the artifact it will produce and where it is kept | … ; if it fails: … | … |\n91\t\n92\tOne row per gate the plan cites, and no others. Every threshold carries its label. Evidence names\n93\tan artifact the check will produce, never a result. Phase may read \"starts in N, required before M\".\n94\t\n95\t## 7. Cross-cutting concerns (per phase, from the first commit)\n96\t\n97\t| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n98\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n99\t| 0 | … | … | … | … |\n100\t\n101\tObservability appears in Phase 0. No cell is empty; where a declared exception bypasses one, cite\n102\tit (E…).\n103\t\n104\t## 8. AI layer (AI/agentic systems only)\n105\t\n106\t| Sublayer | In this system | Built in | Exit check or V-ID |\n107\t|---|---|---|---|\n108\t| 1. Model access | … | … | … |\n113\t| 6. Memory | … | … | … |\n114\t| 7. Orchestration | … | … | … |\n115\t| 8. Routing | … | … | … |\n116\t| 9. Feedback | … | … | … |\n117\t\n118\tA capability sublayer (4–9) this system does not need: \"Not needed — <reason>\". {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01S8zwD7JDYZp3enuLfbtcQy","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n**Phase 0 groundwork:**\n- Inventory the old CI: deploy jobs, cron and batch jobs, artifact consumers, reused credentials. Mark each CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n- Baseline per service: build duration, queue time, deploy frequency, change failure rate, time to restore, and CI spend.\n- Start the IAM approval, the vendor contract, the budget request and the V6 approver now. They have the longest lead time.\n\n**The real request:**\n1. A merge to `main` on one low-criticality, stateless internal service, for example an internal admin API.\n2. A short-lived runner builds and unit-tests it.\n3. The image is pushed to the registry by digest, with an SBOM and a signature.\n4. The bot commits a digest bump to the environment repo: staging first, then prod.\n5. Argo CD in the prod cluster syncs it.\n6. The Kubernetes rollout runs and the health check passes.\n7. A green deploy status appears on the commit.\n\n**Tiers crossed:** source control → CI and runner → registry → environment repo → Argo CD → policy controller (audit mode) → cluster → service.\n\n**Day zero:**\n- **Logged:** pipeline, Argo CD and cluster events go to the existing log stack, correlated by commit SHA and run ID.\n- **Traced:** CI spans are exported over OpenTelemetry, so one trace covers the whole path.\n- **Monitored:** alerts on pipeline failure, Argo CD sync failed or degraded, and runner queue time.\n- **Rollback:** `git revert` of the digest bump, after which Argo CD redeploys the previous digest. Fallback: re-enable the pilot's old deploy job.\n\n**Who can reach it:** only the platform team and the pilot repo, protected `main` only, no secrets for pull requests from forks. Admission policy runs in audit mode, scoped to the pilot namespace.\n\n**Exit check V0:**\n- A real merge reaches prod with one trace across every tier.\n- A deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline.\n- An injected sync failure fires an alert.\n- First values for queue time, duration and lead time are recorded as BASELINE floors, not as capacity.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Trust boundary and supply chain**\n  - **Unlocks:** onboarding repos other than the pilot.\n  - **Depends on:** V0.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Protection on the environment repo: CODEOWNERS, branch protection, bot-only digest bumps.\n    3. Argo CD AppProjects and RBAC per team.\n    4. KMS-backed signing plus provenance.\n    5. Kyverno set to enforce on the pilot namespace.\n    6. Secrets from the secret manager, never stored in CI.\n    7. Runner network policy: no path to production data stores.\n    8. Secret scanning on logs.\n    9. Audit logs sent to the SIEM.\n    10. Run V1.\n  - **Rollback:** policy back to audit mode through a flag; OIDC roles are additive.\n  - **Exit check:** V1 passes.\n\n- **Phase 2: Pipeline contract and runner fleet (shadow mode)**\n  - **Unlocks:** production waves.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 1, V1.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Template v1 and `service.yaml`, with the database migration step.\n    2. Run them alongside the old pipelines on 5 representative services (mixed languages, one stateful with migrations, one unusual build), deploying to staging only. Prod stays on old CI.\n    3. Ring rollout for template versions: pilot → wave → all.\n    4. Runner autoscaling and caching.\n    5. Retention policies.\n    6. Run V2 and V3.\n  - **Rollback:** turn off shadow runs; production is untouched.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V2 and V3 pass.\n    - A bad template change, injected on purpose, stops at the pilot ring.\n\n- **Phase 3: Wave 1 to production, plus progressive delivery and break-glass**\n  - **Unlocks:** wider waves and tier-1 services.\n  - **Depends on:** V2, V3.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Cut over about 8 low-criticality services with the per-service checklist: disable the old job, auto-sync the Argo app, first deploy as a canary with manual promotion, rehearse one rollback.\n    2. Run V4 and V5.\n    6. Close out V6.\n  - **Rollback:** per service, re-enable the old job and disable auto-sync. The old CI stays the system of record until cutover.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V4, V5 and V6 pass.\n    - Each wave-1 service has at least 3 prod deploys, with change failure rate no worse than its BASELINE.\n\n- **Phase 4: Remaining waves, smallest exposure first**\n  - **Unlocks:** decommissioning the old CI.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 3; V4, V5 and V6 before any tier-1 service.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Wave 2: about 15 medium-criticality services.\n    2. Wave 3: about 15 more.\n    3. Wave 4: about 10 tier-1 services, 1–2 at a time.\n    4. Start each wave only after the previous wave's exit check passes.\n    5. Revoke old-CI credentials after each service's 10th successful deploy.\n    6. Set platform SLOs and burn-rate alerts once the UNKNOWN targets arrive.\n  - **Rollback:** per service, as in Phase 3. Once credentials are revoked, the fallback is break-glass.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - All 50 services deploy only through the new path.\n    - Lead time measured against the target set by leadership.\n\n- **Phase 5: Retire the old CI**\n  - **Unlocks:** one deploy path; old credentials gone.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 4, V7.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Re-home the non-deploy jobs found in the Phase 0 inventory.\n    2. Export and archive the old configurations.\n    3. Rehearse restoring one old job from the archive.\n    4. Run V7.\n    5. Delete the old CI.\n  - **Point of no return:** deleting the old CI server and its data, guarded by V7.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V7 passes.\n    - No traffic or credential use against the old CI for 14 days.\n    - The operational-complexity budget holds.\n\n## 6. Database migrations run as a pre-sync job using expand/contract | 5 representative services fit without forking the template | V2 | V2 fails (more than 1 of the 5 needs a fork) → add extension hooks or a second template family per stack |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: personal data or secrets leaked into build logs cannot be recalled | No production data or production secrets in CI; synthetic test data; runners have no network path to production data stores; log masking; 30-day log retention | No test needs production data today (inventory confirms) | V1 | A service needs production-like data → a masked or synthetic dataset pipeline, never raw data |\n| (Brownfield) migration, coexistence, system of record | R2: reversible per service | Replatform the pipelines only; do not change the services. Exactly one authoritative deployer per service: the old CI before cutover, the environment repo after. The old deploy job is disabled, not deleted. A service's old-CI prod credentials are revoked after 10 successful deploys on the new path; from then on the fallback is break-glass | Two deployers never run at once | V0 rollback rehearsal; per-service cutover checklist | A service's cutover fails twice → it goes back to old CI and into a later wave |\n\n**R1 defaults:**\n- Custom platform service vs configuration only → configuration only.\n- Deploy status → async: Argo CD reconciles and reports back as a commit status.\n- Signing → cosign with a KMS key, an SBOM from syft, and SLSA provenance.\n- Policy engine → Kyverno.\n- Environment repo layout → one repo, a directory per service, CODEOWNERS per team.\n- Template updates → version tags bumped by Renovate.\n\n**N/A:**\n- Tenancy model: one organization. Team isolation is handled by Argo CD AppProjects under the deploy-model row.\n- AI rows: no AI component.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n**Phase 0 groundwork:**\n- Inventory the old CI: deploy jobs, cron and batch jobs, artifact consumers, reused credentials. Mark each CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n- Baseline per service: build duration, queue time, deploy frequency, change failure rate, time to restore, and CI spend.\n- Start the IAM approval, the vendor contract, the budget request and the V6 approver now. They have the longest lead time.\n\n**The real request:**\n1. A merge to `main` on one low-criticality, stateless internal service, for example an internal admin API.\n2. A short-lived runner builds and unit-tests it.\n3. The image is pushed to the registry by digest, with an SBOM and a signature.\n4. The bot commits a digest bump to the environment repo: staging first, then prod.\n5. Argo CD in the prod cluster syncs it.\n6. The Kubernetes rollout runs and the health check passes.\n7. A green deploy status appears on the commit.\n\n**Tiers crossed:** source control → CI and runner → registry → environment repo → Argo CD → policy controller (audit mode) → cluster → service.\n\n**Day zero:**\n- **Logged:** pipeline, Argo CD and cluster events go to the existing log stack, correlated by commit SHA and run ID.\n- **Traced:** CI spans are exported over OpenTelemetry, so one trace covers the whole path.\n- **Monitored:** alerts on pipeline failure, Argo CD sync failed or degraded, and runner queue time.\n- **Rollback:** `git revert` of the digest bump, after which Argo CD redeploys the previous digest. Fallback: re-enable the pilot's old deploy job.\n\n**Who can reach it:** only the platform team and the pilot repo, protected `main` only, no secrets for pull requests from forks. Admission policy runs in audit mode, scoped to the pilot namespace.\n\n**Exit check V0:**\n- A real merge reaches prod with one trace across every tier.\n- A deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline.\n- An injected sync failure fires an alert.\n- First values for queue time, duration and lead time are recorded as BASELINE floors, not as capacity.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Trust boundary and supply chain**\n  - **Unlocks:** onboarding repos other than the pilot.\n  - **Depends on:** V0.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Per-repo OIDC roles, and per-service registry paths that only that repo's `main` identity can write.\n    2. Protection on the environment repo: CODEOWNERS, branch protection, bot-only digest bumps.\n    3. Argo CD AppProjects and RBAC per team.\n    4. KMS-backed signing plus provenance.\n    5. Kyverno set to enforce on the pilot namespace.\n    6. Secrets from the secret manager, never stored in CI.\n    7. Runner network policy: no path to production data stores.\n    8. Secret scanning on logs.\n    9. Audit logs sent to the SIEM.\n    10. Run V1.\n  - **Rollback:** policy back to audit mode through a flag; OIDC roles are additive.\n  - **Exit check:** V1 passes.\n\n- **Phase 2: Pipeline contract and runner fleet (shadow mode)**\n  - **Unlocks:** production waves.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 1, V1.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Template v1 and `service.yaml`, with the database migration step.\n    2. Run them alongside the old pipelines on 5 representative services (mixed languages, one stateful with migrations, one unusual build), deploying to staging only. Prod stays on old CI.\n    3. Ring rollout for template versions: pilot → wave → all.\n    4. Runner autoscaling and caching.\n    5. Retention policies.\n    6. Run V2 and V3.\n  - **Rollback:** turn off shadow runs; production is untouched.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V2 and V3 pass.\n    - A bad template change, injected on purpose, stops at the pilot ring.\n\n- **Phase 3: Wave 1 to production, plus progressive delivery and break-glass**\n  - **Unlocks:** wider waves and tier-1 services.\n  - **Depends on:** V2, V3.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Cut over about 8 low-criticality services with the per-service checklist: disable the old job, auto-sync the Argo app, first deploy as a canary with manual promotion, rehearse one rollback.\n    2. Add Argo Rollouts canary analysis on request-rate, error and latency metrics.\n    3. Build break-glass and the registry mirror.\n    4. Staff the platform on-call rotation.\n    5. Run V4 and V5.\n    6. Close out V6.\n  - **Rollback:** per service, re-enable the old job and disable auto-sync. The old CI stays the system of record until cutover.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V4, V5 and V6 pass.\n    - Each wave-1 service has at least 3 prod deploys, with change failure rate no worse than its BASELINE.\n\n- **Phase 4: Remaining waves, smallest exposure first**\n  - **Unlocks:** decommissioning the old CI.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 3; V4, V5 and V6 before any tier-1 service.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Wave 2: about 15 medium-criticality services.\n    2. Wave 3: about 15 more.\n    3. Wave 4: about 10 tier-1 services, 1–2 at a time.\n    4. Start each wave only after the previous wave's exit check passes.\n    5. Revoke old-CI credentials after each service's 10th successful deploy.\n    6. Set platform SLOs and burn-rate alerts once the UNKNOWN targets arrive.\n  - **Rollback:** per service, as in Phase 3. Once credentials are revoked, the fallback is break-glass.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - All 50 services deploy only through the new path.\n    - Lead time measured against the target set by leadership.\n\n- **Phase 5: Retire the old CI**\n  - **Unlocks:** one deploy path; old credentials gone.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 4, V7.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Re-home the non-deploy jobs found in the Phase 0 inventory.\n    2. Export and archive the old configurations.\n    3. Rehearse restoring one old job from the archive.\n    4. Run V7.\n    5. Delete the old CI.\n  - **Point of no return:** deleting the old CI server and its data, guarded by V7.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V7 passes.\n    - No traffic or credential use against the old CI for 14 days.\n    - The operational-complexity budget holds.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in production | The pilot run in §4 | The V0 exit check in §4 | Run link, trace export, revert commit, alert record, baseline sheet in `platform/evidence/V0` | Phase 1 | 0 |\n| V1 | A compromised CI job in any repo cannot deploy to prod, tamper with another service, or reach production data | Red-team test from a feature-branch job and a fork pull request. Try to: read deploy credentials, push to another service's registry path, write the prod path in the environment repo, deploy an unsigned image, reach a production database. Then a design review | All 5 attempts fail, and the security lead signs off (pass/fail) | Red-team report, policy-deny logs and the review record in the security repo | Phase 2. If it fails: fix and re-test; persistent failure flips the deploy-model row | 1 |\n| V2 | One versioned template fits the variety of services | Put the 5 representative services on template v1 in shadow mode for 2 weeks | No forks in at least 4 of 5; image outputs match the old pipeline's tests | Shadow-run report per service in the platform repo | Freeze and version v1; Phase 3. If it fails: extension hooks or template families | 2 |\n| V3 | The runner fleet meets queue time, duration and cost at scale | Replay the BASELINE peak-hour job mix at 2× for 1 hour; 2 weeks of real shadow load | Queue p95 < 2 min (ASSUMPTION); duration ≤ 1.1× BASELINE (ASSUMPTION); projected monthly cost at 50 services ≤ budget (UNKNOWN: finance supplies it by the end of Phase 0) | Load-test report and cost projection | Reserved capacity; Phase 3. If it fails: caching, hosted runners, or re-plan the build-vs-buy row | 2 |\n| V4 | A canary catches a bad release and rolls back automatically | 3 injected bad releases (error fault behind a test flag) at 10% canary on wave-1 internal services, plus at least 20 good releases | 3 of 3 aborted; traffic back on stable ≤ 10 min (ASSUMPTION); at most 1 false abort in 20 | Rollouts analysis runs and the timeline export | Automated canary for tier-1. If it fails: tier-1 uses manual promotion with a named approver | 3 |\n| V5 | A hotfix can ship during a platform outage, and a policy-controller outage does not stop the cluster | Game day: block source control and CI SaaS; an on-call engineer who did not build the platform deploys the previous digest and a pre-signed hotfix through break-glass. Also kill the policy controller | Within 60 min (ASSUMPTION) with a complete audit record; system namespaces unaffected; alert within 5 min | Game-day log and the audit trail export | Tier-1 waves and credential revocation. If it fails: tier-1 stays on old CI | 3 |\n| V6 | Pipeline records count as approved change evidence | Review of PR approvals, provenance and Argo CD audit logs against the change policy | Pass/fail sign-off by the change manager or compliance lead (UNKNOWN who: eng leadership names them in Phase 0) | Signed decision record | Tier-1 waves. If it fails: an explicit prod-approval step in the environment-repo PR | starts 0, required before 4 |\n| V7 | Retiring the old CI breaks nothing and loses nothing | Inventory reconciliation, 14 days of zero use, restore rehearsal | Every inventory item re-homed or retired; zero calls or credential use for 14 days; one job restored from the archive; go/no-go by the platform lead and the VP Eng | Reconciliation sheet, access-log export, rehearsal record | Deletion. If it fails: keep the old CI read-only and fix the gaps | 5 |\n\n## 7. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | Protected `main` only; no secrets for fork pull requests; policy in audit mode | One correlated trace and logs across tiers; 3 alerts; baselines | Platform kept as code (Terraform plus Helm); digest-pinned images | Rollback rehearsed; old job kept as fallback |\n| 1 | OIDC, signing, enforced admission, network isolation, SIEM | Policy-deny and audit-log dashboards | Provenance attestations; pinned action and tool versions | Policy webhook HA; system namespaces excluded |\n| 2 | Shadow runs on a non-prod registry path only; SBOM vulnerability scan (warn only) | Queue, duration and cost dashboards per service | Versioned templates; build once, promote by digest | Ring rollout for templates; runner autoscaling |\n| 3 | Break-glass with two-person key and audit | Canary analysis metrics; deploy status per service | Per-service cutover checklist kept as code | Break-glass, registry mirror, platform on-call (V5) |\n| 4 | Revoke old credentials per service | SLOs and burn-rate alerts; lead-time and change-failure dashboard | Template version spread report (who is behind) | Waves with one-at-a-time tier-1 cutover |\n| 5 | Old credentials and server destroyed | Watch for any old-CI use for 14 days | Archived old configurations | Restore rehearsal before the point of no return |\n\n## 8. Deliberately deferred\n- **Developer portal (for example, Backstage):** when platform support requests outgrow the platform team's capacity.\n- **Preview environment per pull request:** when contention for staging is measured as a delivery bottleneck.\n- **Multi-cluster or multi-region fleet management (ApplicationSets):** when a second production cluster or region exists.\n- **SLSA L3 hermetic builds:** when audit scope requires it, or the V1 review flags a provenance gap.\n- **Blocking builds on vulnerabilities:** when the false-positive rate from warn-only mode is measured and accepted by the security lead.\n- **Remote build cache service:** when V3's duration check fails or comes close to failing.\n- **Automated canary for services without standard metrics:** as each service starts emitting request-rate, error and latency metrics.","ttft_ms":3328,"type":"result","duration_ms":281646,"uuid":"4f40b1bd-adde-4afb-86f7-66b62882dc4d","ttft_stream_ms":2369,"time_to_request_ms":242,"first_content_frame_ms":2370,"queued_turn_count":0,"result_index":0}
